opus-5.5.text:
Not very dogmatic at all, honestly. I think dogmatism about methods is one of the faster ways to get stuck in a field like this, because olfaction is still so underexplored computationally. We don't have the luxury of decades of benchmarks the way vision or language do.

What I *am* dogmatic about is the problem. I care about whether we can actually predict what a molecule smells like, whether those predictions hold up when you put them in front of trained human panelists, and whether they generalize to molecules nobody has ever smelled before. That's the bar. The model is just a means to get there.

In practice, graph neural networks have turned out to be a really natural fit, because molecules *are* graphs: atoms are nodes, bonds are edges, and you can learn representations directly from that structure instead of hand-engineering descriptors. That's worked well for us, and the embeddings we've learned seem to capture something real about perceptual space, since they transfer to related tasks we didn't explicitly train on.

But if tomorrow someone showed me that a simpler model with better data beat it, or that some transformer-style architecture over molecular representations did better, I'd switch happily. Honestly, a lot of the gains in this area come from the data side: getting cleaner, more consistent odor labels, dealing with the fact that human descriptions of smell are noisy and culturally loaded, and thinking hard about evaluation. The architecture matters, but it's rarely the only bottleneck.

So I'd say: firm on the goal, firm on rigorous evaluation against real human perception, and pretty flexible about everything in between.

r001.rationale: The response says the speaker is firm about the goal and evaluation, while flexible about modeling methods. It mentions data quality but does not identify data size and quality as the focus of dogmatic commitment.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, not very dogmatic at all, and I think that's been important for us. When we started, there was a real temptation to just take whatever architecture was winning on vision or language at the moment and bolt it onto molecules. We tried a lot of that. What we found is that smell has some pretty specific structure that you have to respect, and the modeling choice should follow from that rather than from what's fashionable.

So, for example, molecules are naturally graphs. Atoms are nodes, bonds are edges. That pointed us toward graph neural networks pretty early, and they did well on predicting odor descriptors from structure. But I'd be the first to say the GNN itself isn't the point. What matters is that the model can learn a representation where molecules that smell similar end up close together, even when their structures look quite different to a chemist. That's the actual problem. If a transformer or some other architecture gets us there better, great, we'll use it.

The other thing that keeps me from being dogmatic is that the data is the bottleneck far more than the model. Olfaction doesn't have an ImageNet. Our labels come from trained human panels, and those are noisy, expensive, and culturally loaded. People in different places use different words for the same smell. So a huge amount of our effort goes into how we collect data, how we calibrate panelists, how we think about the sensor side of things. A fancier architecture on bad labels gets you nowhere.

Where I am a bit stubborn is on the goal. I want models that generalize to molecules no one has ever smelled, because that's where the scientific and practical value is. If a method only interpolates within the known fragrance catalog, I'm not that interested, no matter how elegant it is. So I'd say I'm flexible on the how and pretty rigid on the what.

r001.rationale: The response says the modeling approach is flexible and data is a bottleneck, describing label quality issues. But it identifies generalization as the speaker’s stubborn commitment, not data size and quality.

astra-6.text:
I'm not particularly dogmatic about the modeling approach. I'm much more dogmatic about whether it works: does it predict what something smells like, and does that prediction hold up when you test it on new molecules?

There are useful inductive biases you can bring to the problem. Molecules have structure, so models that can represent that structure are a natural place to start. But I don't think we should commit to a particular architecture as the answer to olfaction. We should let the experiments tell us which approaches are useful, and be willing to change our minds.

r001.rationale: The response says its dogmatic focus is whether a model predicts smell and generalizes to new molecules. It does not identify data size or quality as the focus.

If a simple model works, great. If we need a graph neural network or something more complex, that's fine too. Biology gives us a lot of inspiration, but I don't think we have to reproduce the olfactory system in every detail to build something useful.
